Waste Management Appendix Appendix 1 One Resin: Many Properties and Many Applications Bakelite is a resin discovered as a substitute for natural resources like shellac and rubber. It is essentially an adhesive. Let's take a look at its primary uses.

Plywood Manufacturing Thin sheets of wood (veneers) are cut from softwood using machinery. Each layer is then dipped in Bakelite adhesive and placed on top of one another. They are compressed under high heat to form a single sheet, resulting in plywood. This is the process of plywood manufacturing. Other Applications In addition to plywood products, Bakelite is widely used in industries such A01 as electronics and electricals, laminate manufacturing, aerospace, ballistics, railway manufacturing, automotive production, and construction. Bakelite plastic is valued for its transparency when made into thin sheets. Other key properties include being lightweight, heat resistance, chemical resistance, electrical insulation, moldability in any form, durability, and the ability to add various colours. Why Thermoset? When left in the soil for an extended period, Bakelite undergoes limited biodegradation.

However, it is not suitable for recycling to recover materials. For this reason, it is classified as a thermoset resin. Bakelite can withstand temperatures up to 300°C without undergoing significant chemical or physical changes. As such, products made from this resin are durable and long-lasting even after prolonged use. Such resin products, due to their long-lasting nature, leave relatively limited residues (RDF - Refuse Derived Fuel) after their use. These residues can only be incinerated in cement kilns to convert them into energy for utilization. Through Green Technology

Melamine Resin The manufacturing process of melamine resin is similar to that of Bakelite. If phenol is replaced with melamine, melamine-formaldehyde resin is produced. Melamine resin is widely used for laminates intended for various applications, such as Formica, dinnerware, cooking utensils, plates, and laminate flooring. It also serves as a plasticizer added to concrete. With excellent insulating properties and fire resistance, melamine resin is also used in paints.

Urea Formaldehyde If urea replaces phenol in Bakelite manufacturing, urea-formaldehyde resin is obtained. The three types of resins share many similarities in their properties. The New Era of Petroplastics In 1920, Hermann Staudinger, a German organic chemist, revolutionized synthetic polymers with his new definitions and the chemical process of polymerization (Uber Polymerisation), marking the birth of petroplastics. Early products of petroleum-based plastics include PVC (1926), Polyethylene (1933), Nylon-6 (1935), and Polystyrene (1935). However, the most significant growth A02 and development occurred with olefin polymers, known as Polyethylene or ethylene polymers. These are recyclable polymers, which can be melted at suitable temperatures (between 100°C and 160°C) to create new products. Hence, they are referred to as thermoplastics.

Appendix 2 Incineration is Appropriate, Not Open Burning Various materials are used in the manufacturing of diapers and sanitary pads. The primary substance is SAP (Super Absorbent Polymer), which has excellent moisture-absorbing capabilities. Common SAPs include sodium polyacrylate, sodium polyacrylamide, cellulose-acrylonitrile copolymer, and cellulose-maleic anhydride copolymer. These are enclosed in plastic outer layers. The moisture- absorbing surface consists of porous polypropylene sheets. On the other hand, the material that prevents moisture from escaping is a polyethylene film. These films are difficult to incinerate at normal temperatures. By law, only incinerators should be used for this purpose. However, the incinerator should not be used in a manner that emits excessive smoke.
Sanitary waste must be deposited in the furnace only after ensuring that the furnace temperature has exceeded the ignition point of the materials being incinerated. Under such

conditions, smoke emission will be minimal, combustion will be efficient, and the disposal method will be safe. Refer to the table showing the melting points of various plastics for more information. Let us examine the combustion process more scientifically. After the water content in used sanitary pads evaporates as steam, the organic matter they contain will burn easily. The remaining materials are the structural components of the pad. These include polypropylene and polyethylene films, as previously mentioned. Both are polymers with unique melting and ignition points. Polypropylene melts above 158°C, and its ignition point is above 328°C. Polyethylene, on the other hand, melts above 107°C and ignites above 349°C. Then there is SAP (Super Absorbent Polymer), primarily sodium polyacrylate (SPA). Its properties are as follows: it can absorb 100 to 1,000 times its weight in moisture.
Once the moisture evaporates as steam, SPA melts and vaporizes above 150°C. However, SPA is a non-flammable polymer.

Appendix 3 Modern Processing Methods: E-Waste and Battery Waste Sectors A03 The modern methods of processing e-waste include the following: Pyrometallurgical Method Pyrometallurgy is a technique that recovers metals through thermal processing. We are already familiar with the concentration of e-waste. The metal-rich fractions obtained after shredding and sorting are subjected to thermal processing. This process consists of three stages: heating, smelting, and cooling. Equipment such as furnaces, incinerators, and plasma arcs is used for thermal processing. The initial stage is combustion or burning, also referred to as conflagration. This is followed by pyrolysis. The temperature can rise up to 700°C during this process. This is the phase where plastics melt, creating carbon compounds that burn off and become non-toxic. The heat released during this stage helps increase the temperature of the smelter.
Simultaneously, certain metals within this temperature range vaporize. These gases are collected via flue gas, converted into metal compounds, and subsequently processed to recover the metals.

The next stage of the process involves incineration, where the furnace temperature can rise to 2000°C or even higher depending on the smelter's capacity. In thermal treatment methods, a plasma arc furnace can be used to achieve such high temperatures. Observe the melting points of various metals in the table below. Melting Points of Metals < 500°C < 1000°C < 1500°C < 2000°C < 3500°C Ga 30 Sb 631 Au 1064 Fe 1538 Ta 3020 Li 180.5 Pa 220-260 Al 660 Cu 1085 Ti 1668 W 3422 Sn 232 As 817 Mn 1246 Pt 1768 Bi 272 Ge 938 Be 1287 Cr 1907 Cd 321 Ag 961 Ni 1455 Rh 1964 Pb 328 Zn 420 Te 450 A04 During the melting phase, certain metals (e.g., Lithium, Cadmium, Lead, Copper, Zinc, Palladium, Chromium) vaporize and can be recovered via flue gas. Other metals settle separately and eventually form into slag. The process of separating a specific metal from its accompanying materials is known as drossing.

Another phenomenon occurring alongside this is sintering, where metal particles scattered across the furnace fuse together into a mass when they approach their melting point. This allows them to be recovered as solid metals or alloys. Metals in e-waste that cannot vaporize can be recovered using sintering based on their respective melting points.

Hydrometallurgical Method The hydrometallurgical method is a technology used to purify the various metals recovered in the form of flue gas, slag, or alloys. The first step involves separating each type of metal into water-soluble salts. Suitable concentrated acids and related chemical compounds are required for this process. Metals are then separated from the solution through electrolysis. This process is called electro-refining. In the electrolytic process, metal ions in

the solution combine with electrons and deposit at the anode. The process of purifying and extracting metals is known as the electrometallurgical process. Appendix 4 Hydrogen Fuel Cell A hydrogen fuel cell converts the chemical energy stored in hydrogen and oxygen molecules into electrical energy. This process occurs at a temperature of 25°C. The usable voltage from the fuel cell ranges between 0.6 volts and 1.2 volts. Unlike other cells, fuel cells do not have energy storage capabilities. The cell functions only when hydrogen is supplied to it. This is what differentiates hydrogen fuel cells from other types of cells. The structure of a fuel cell is similar to that of other cells, comprising three main components: The anode (-), The cathode (+), The electrolyte layer between them. These components are enclosed within a protective outer casing. Anode (-) The anode is a gas diffusion electrode.

The hydrogen gas that enters the anode chamber reacts with the electrode in a A05 gas diffusion layer, which ensures that hydrogen gas effectively reaches the (+) a t h ode electrode. The anode is made of Platinum. C d e (-) Its composition includes nanoscale An o Platinum particles combined with a proton-conducting polymer, allowing it to function effectively. The anode breaks down hydrogen molecules into protons and electrons.

Cathode (+) The cathode consists of a porous carbon rod surface coated with nanoscale platinum particles and a proton-conducting polymer mixture. It has a structure similar to the anode. The oxygen in the air entering this section combines with protons here, supported by the gas diffusion layer. Additionally, the cathode enables the inclusion of the flow of electrons entering through an external electric wire into the above-mentioned combination. The reaction occurring at the cathode is as follows: 2H⁺ + ½ O₂ + 2e⁻ → H₂O + heat The resultant release of water vapour, unused air, and residual oxygen that remains as by-products of the reaction is also processed in the cathode. Reference 1 Plastics and the Environment When it comes to the use of plastics, the saying "too much of a good thing A06 can be harmful" is literally true. There was a surge in the plastic production sector to create the best and all-encompassing products, which bypassed all restrictions, leading to significant environmental concerns. According to United Nations estimates, the total amount of plastic produced globally between 1950 and 2015 amounts to 8.3 billion tons. More than three-quarters of this, i.e., 6.3 billion tons, constitutes plastic waste discarded after use. Of this, over the 65-year period, only 567 million tons (9%) were recycled. Approximately 12%, or 756 million tons of plastic waste, has been openly incinerated during the aforementioned period. The remaining 79%, which amounts to 4.977 billion tons, of plastic waste has been deposited across oceans and land.
These plastic residues, capable of persisting without degrading for decades, cause significant environmental damage (NITI Aayog - UNDP Handbook on

Waste Management Sustainable Urban Plastic Waste Management - 2021). According to the 2022 assessment by the UN Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee, global plastic production in 2021 alone was 430 million tons. Of this, 66% (approximately 256 million tons) consisted of products designed for short-term use. These can primarily be categorized into three groups: 1. Packaging plastics 2. Single-Use Plastics (SUP) 3. Other miscellaneous plastics The first two categories—SUP and packaging plastics—accounted for 155 million tons (36%) of global production in 2021. Current estimates suggest that approximately 5 billion tons of plastic waste have accumulated in the oceans. From this, around 500,000 tons of microplastics (tiny shards less than five millimeters in size) are A07 released annually, causing harm to marine life. The UNDP estimates that 100,000 ton of marine mammals die annually due to this pollution.

According to studies by the Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), India produces approximately 20 million tons of plastic products annually, equating to around 14 kilograms per capita. As per the Central Pollution Control Board, urban areas in India alone generated 3.47 million tons of plastic waste in 2019–2020. It is also estimated that half of the materials used for packaging purposes in India are made of plastic. Through Green Technology

Dear children, We are journeying through an era of constant changes, where new kinds of technologies are emerging every day. You will step into a new world completely different from the one you entered when you began your studies. We are surrounded by new knowledge wherever we go. While it is not at all difficult to discover this knowledge, it is necessary to gain expertise in certain professional fields if we are to survive in this new world. The scientific method involves forming new ideas, acquiring skills and abilities to implement them, and then testing them. Therefore, while learning various subjects is important, you should also create opportunities to gain in-depth knowledge and experience in your areas of interest. This is the aim of vocational education. There are various opportunities to get acquainted with various skill sets and engage in practical activities integrated with other subjects from grade five onwards.

The activity books are designed so that in Grade 9, students can focus more on their area of interest, participate in related activities, and gain skills. Unit Chit Funds 1 Pic 1.1 Parthan, a software engineer, runs a small startup. He decided to buy a car worth ₹6,00,000 as it was essential for improving his business operations. He paid ₹1,00,000 in cash and took a loan of ₹5,00,000 at an interest rate of 9%. The monthly repayment for the loan was ₹10,830. Currently, Parthan has a chit fund worth ₹5,00,000. Six months after buying the car, he received ₹4,50,000 from this chit fund. After six months of buying the car, he has already paid ₹10,830 each month for the loan repayment, he still needs to repay approximately ₹4,48,000 for the remaining loan amount.

What financial considerations might Parthan have in this scenario? Could you discuss and present them? Let’s explore the possible concerns that might come to your mind. Possibility 1 : Repay the loan completely using the chit fund. Possibility 2 : Continue with both the loan repayment and the chit fund, and invest the amount received from the chit in a 3-year investment with an 8% interest rate. Possibility 3 : Pay off the car loan completely using the chit fund and join a new chit fund by using the monthly instalment of the car loan. What other options might come to your mind in this situation? Which one do you think is the most appropriate? Could you help Parthan choose the most suitable financial decision? Here, we need to understand what a chit fund is and its unique features. To gain 8 more insight into chit funds, let’s meet Jeevan, who has been working for many years at KSFE, a State owned financial enterprise in Kerala.

Let’s hear what he has to say. Chit funds in India operate under the Chit Funds Act passed in 1982. They are known by different names, such as chit, chit fund, or ‘kuri’. In this system, a person enters into an agreement with a group of people where all participants commit to pay a fixed amount in regular instalments over a specified period. According to the agreement, each member is entitled to receive the chit amount. This can be decided through various methods, such as lot, an auction, or any other procedure specified in the agreement. For example, KSFE starts a chit with a total value of ₹4 lakh (Sala). To form this chit, 50 members are required to contribute ₹8,000 each month for 50 months. The company collects ₹4 lakh from these 50 members, with each contributing ₹8,000 per month. This amount is then given to one of the subscribers after deducting a commission (for example, 5%).

If more than one subscriber is interested in receiving the chit amount, lot or an auction will be held. The subscriber willing to accept a lower amount than others will be chosen. However, they will have to bear a higher commission deduction (for example, 30%) from the total chit value. This ensures that the subscriber receives the chit amount at a reduced value while accounting for the higher commission fee. The deducted amount (after the commission) is then distributed among the other members as compound interest. As a result, the members only need to pay the remaining amount after the compound interest is allocated to them. The special feature of this system is that all the 50 members will receive their chit amount during the 50-month duration, ensuring that every participant benefits from the chit. Multi-Division Chits In a typical chit fund, only one subscriber wins the chit amount through a lot or auction each month. However, in multi-division chits, one lucky subscriber receives 95% of the chit value (after deducting the 5% foreman’s commission), while the remaining subscribers get their chits through an auction at a lower value. For example, in a scheme with 400 subscribers and 4 divisions, one subscriber may receive the chit amount each month after deducting the 5% foreman’s commission, while the other three get their chits through auction at a lower value. Multi-division chits allow both lottery and auction-based participation, making them a popular option, particularly in KSFE.

History of Chits Centuries ago, in many villages of Kerala, farmers would contribute a fixed amount of money or grains every month to a trusted person in their village. This trustee would help any member of the group in need by collecting the required resources. The origin of the term “chit fund” comes from the word “chit,” that means a paper token. Chit funds have existed since ancient times as a way for people in need of money to raise funds. In 1887, William Logan, the former collector of the Malabar district in the Madras Presidency, mentioned that chit funds were commonly practised among friendly groups in that region. During this period, chit funds were also used to collect money for special events such as weddings in South India. In the 1930s, 166 banks in Kerala were conducting chit funds. The first government-run chit fund, Kerala State Financial Enterprise (KSFE), was established by the Kerala government in 1969.
The concept of chit funds, which is uniquely Indian, is now practised globally. Activity 1 Prepare an Advertisement for Chits

Are chits a better option than loans? Joining a chit fund with future needs in mind can be a more beneficial financial 12 option compared to a loan. Utilising the chit amount at the right time helps avoid taking a loan and repaying it with interest, thus eliminating repayment liability. Some subscribers remain in the chit without participating in the lot or auction, but the financial benefits are lower in such cases. The amount won in the chit auction can be invested as a fixed deposit to earn profit. Chits can be used as a profitable financial resource by choosing the right ones, based on an individual’s financial goals and capacity of monthly payments.

Activity 2 Are There any Laws to Regulate the Operation of Chit Funds? The Central Government introduced the Chit Fund Act in 1982 to regulate the operation of chit funds. In Kerala, although the Kerala Chit Fund Rules of 2012 and their subsequent amendment in 2016 were initially in existence, the central law has now been made applicable to all the chit funds in the state. According to this law, anyone intending to start or operate a chit fund must obtain prior permission from the state government. This means that all the chit funds are required to be registered under the State Registration Department. However, despite these regulations, unregistered chit funds continue to exist in certain areas. Joining such unregistered chit funds may lead to risks such as fraud or breaches of contract.

Chit fund organisations are not required to be registered under the Reserve Bank of India regulations, but chit fund companies are regulated as MNBC (Miscellaneous Non-Banking Companies). Their activities related to accepting investments are governed by the Non-Banking Financial Companies Act, 1997 and the Companies Act of 1956/2013. In Kerala, at the government level, KSFE, along with cooperative banks in the cooperative sector and private sector institutions ranging from community organizations to large companies, are active in the chit fund sector. In recent times, businesses like jewellers, furniture/electronic shops, and others have started conducting special purpose chit funds to promote the sales of their products.

Banks and financial institutions provide loans for various other purposes apart from home loans. Let’s Understand in Detail about the Loan Finance Loans are a way of borrowing money to meet various financial needs. The amount borrowed comes with a fixed interest rate and is repaid over time according to a contract. This is a common method of securing funds when individuals or businesses do not have enough money for their needs. Loans are required for various purposes, such as higher education, starting a business, and purchasing cars and houses. There are various types of loans, such as personal loans, education loans, and business loans, each tailored to meet specific requirements.

When availing a loan, it is crucial to carefully evaluate the terms, including interest rate, repayment schedule, loan amount, and collateral. While loans provide a means to achieve goals more quickly, they should be handled wisely to avoid falling into debt. Let us Understand the Different Types of Loans from the Table Provided below: 1 Education Loans Education loans are designed specifically to support students in meeting the expenses of their higher education. These loans cover a range of costs, including tuition fees, books, and other essential study materials. Generally, the repayment begins one year after the com- pletion of the course. To encourage education loans, governments often provide subsidies and tax benefits, making them more accessible and affordable for students.

2 Home Loans These loans are provided to individuals for purchasing or constructing a house. Typically, up to 90% of the property's value can be availed as a loan. The repayment is made in monthly instalments over a period ranging from 10 to 30 years. To encourage house construction, the government offers tax benefits on home loans. 3 Vehicle Loans These loans are provided for purchasing cars, motorcycles, or other vehicles. Typically, up to 80% to 90% of the vehicle's cost is financed through the loan. The borrower repays the loan in fixed monthly instalments over a specified period, usually up to seven years. The purchased vehicle itself serves as collateral for the loan. 4 Gold Loan Borrowers pledge their gold jewellery or gold coins to obtain money. The loan amount is usually 70% to 80% of the market value of the gold. Gold loans are highly popular due to their quick availability, minimal paperwork, and flexible repayment options.
Once the loan and interest are fully repaid, the gold is returned to the borrower.

5 Agricultural Loans These loans are designed to support farmers in meeting essential agricultural needs, including purchasing seeds, fertilizers, farming equipment, and expanding cultivation. They also enable farmers to adopt modern technologies and irrigation systems, improving productivity and efficiency. The key advantages of agricultural loans include low interest rates, simplified procedures, flexible repayment options, and government subsidies. By providing timely financial assistance, these loans play a vital role in promoting agricultural development, enhancing food security. 6 Business Loans These are financial aids provided by financial institutions to meet business needs. They can be utilised for purposes such as business expansion, purchasing equipment, increasing 22 working capital, or starting new projects.

The type of loan and its terms often depend on factors such as the size of the business, credit score, and the purpose of the loan. Business loans are instrumental in fostering industrial growth and, in turn, contributing to national development. 7 Personal Loans These are unsecured loans provided to individuals to meet various personal needs such as debt settlement, medical expenses, home maintenance, or other personal requirements. Personal loans typically have higher interest rates compared to other types of loans. Factors such as the borrower's credit score, income level, and financial history influence the loan amount, repayment conditions, and applicable interest rates. Table 2.1

Equated Monthly Instalments - EMI The amount that a borrower must repay each month on a fixed date is referred to as the ‘Equated Monthly Installment’ (EMI). This amount includes both the interest and the principal components of the loan. The loan is fully repaid by paying the EMI every month over a specified period. If the interest is calculated on the flat-rate method, where the same interest is charged on the total loan amount for the entire loan tenure, calculating EMI is simple. However, if the interest is calculated using the reducing balance method, where interest is charged only on the remaining loan amount after each payment, more calculations are required to determine the EMI. To simplify this process, online EMI calculators are available.

For example, on the SBI website (sbi.co.in/web/student-platform), you can enter the loan details such as amount, interest rate, and tenure into the EMI calculator to calculate the monthly repayment for an educational loan. What is a Credit Card? Credit card is a facility that allows the consumer to borrow money up to a limit predetermined by the bank. Similar to debit cards, credit cards can be used for withdrawing money and shopping. The amount spent using the credit card typically needs to be repaid to the bank on a monthly basis. If the amount is not paid in full, interest at a high Pic 2.5 rate will be charged on the outstanding balance. When shopping with a credit card, benefits like cashback, reward points, discounts, and travel perks are available. However, failing to make timely repayments can lead

to very high interest rates and a drop in the credit score. A decrease in the credit score may eventually prevent access to bank loans in the future. What are the benefits of using Credit Cards? 1. Convenient Use: It eliminates the need to carry large amounts of cash. It makes purchasing goods easier both online and in physical stores. 2. Improved Credit Score: Responsible use of credit cards helps create a good credit score, which is favorable for future loans. 3. Rewards and Cashback: Most credit cards offer benefits like cashback, reward points, and discounts when shopping. 4. Protection from Fraud: Credit cards are issued with enhanced security features. These features help protect users from unauthorised transactions and frauds. 5. Interest-Free Period: If the balance is paid in full within a specified period, no interest is charged on the amount used. It can be considered as a short-term 25 interest-free loan.

6. Emergency Funds: In situations where liquid cash is unavailable, credit cards serve as an emergency source of funds. 7. Global Acceptance: Credit cards are internationally recognised. It can be used for foreign travel and global financial transactions. 8. Expense Tracking: Credit card statements provide a detailed record of expenses, which helps users track and manage their spending. What is a Credit Score? A credit score is a numerical indicator of an individual’s credit worthiness or ability to repay debts. It is determined based on a person’s loan history and repayment behavior with financial institutions. This score, often referred to as credit rating, typically consists of three digits. Which Credit Scores are Used in India? In India, there are four credit rating companies approved by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). z CIBIL (Credit Information Bureau of India Limited) z Experian z Equifax

z High Mark Among these, CIBIL is the most widely used credit score in India. It ranges from 300 to 900, with a score of 750 or above being considered highly desirable. CIBIL Score The full form of CIBIL is Credit Information Bureau India Limited. It is a credit information company that maintains records of all credit-related activities of individuals and organisations. CIBIL is the first bureau in India to start operations as a credit information company in 2000. The credit score calculated by this institution is known as the CIBIL score. In 2017, after TransUnion acquired the company, the CIBIL credit score was renamed to ‘TransUnion CIBIL’. Score Range Rating 300-550 Poor 550-650 Average 650-750 Good 750-900 Excellent

Why is a High Credit Score Important? Banks use the credit score to assess whether an individual is eligible for a loan. The better a person’s credit score, the higher the chances of getting the loan approved. Individuals with a high credit score enjoy benefits such as lower interest rates, favorable repayment terms, and quicker loan approval.

How to Improve Your CIBIL Score? It may be surprising to you that a student’s application for a higher education loan was rejected due to a low CIBIL score. Just as a high academic score helps in gaining admission to higher studies, a high credit score increases the chances of loan approval. A low credit score marks you as a risky borrower who doesn’t repay debts. Pic 2.6

Pic 2.9 Did you notice the collage of news articles provided here? You must have read news like these regarding loan scams. In today’s world, money and financial transactions have become an integral part of our daily lives. Unfortunately, with the growth of technology and online banking, financial frauds, including loan scams, have also been on the rise. Fraudsters deceive people by stealing money through loan scams or by offering loans with unfair terms to exploit them. These scams often begin through phone calls, e-mails, websites, and text messages. They primarily target individuals who do not rely on legitimate banking practices

and are in urgent need of money. Fraudsters promise quick loan approvals with no credit checks and low-interest rates without any hidden fees. However, their real goal may be to steal your money, personal information, or put you in debt. It is essential for students to be aware of such financial frauds, especially loan scams. Understanding how these scams work and how to identify them will help you avoid becoming a victim and also provide you with the knowledge to guide others to stay alert. The fundamental idea that no one engages in business without the intention of making financial gains is the same approach we must consider when it comes to loan scams. How to Stay Vigilant Against Loan Scams? Here are some tips to protect yourself from fraudulent loan apps and loan scams:

1. Ensure Credibility: Always verify the legitimacy of the lender or loan app. Check their website, customer reviews, and ensure they are registered with the 31 RBI. 2. Avoid Prepayment Fees: Legal lenders do not ask for upfront fees for loan approval. Avoid lenders who request prepayment. 3. Do Not Grant Unnecessary Permissions: Be cautious of loan apps that ask for unnecessary permissions, such as access to your contacts, photos, or location. Scammers might misuse this information. 4. Read Terms and Conditions Carefully: Always read the loan agreements, terms, and conditions thoroughly. Fraudulent lenders often include hidden excessive fees or penalties in small print. 5. Be Wary of Unrealistic Offers: Be suspicious of loan offers with extremely low-interest rates or no credit checks. Such offers often turn out to be scams. 6.
Keep Personal Information Secure: Never share sensitive personal or financial information, such as PAN, Aadhaar, or bank account details, with unverified apps or websites.

7. Verify Contact Information: Genuine companies will provide clear contact details such as office address, customer service number, and email. Fraudulent companies often avoid providing reliable contact information. 8. Use Official App Stores: Only download loan apps from official sources like Google Play Store or Apple App Store. 9. Check Customer Ratings: Check user reviews and ratings before using any loan app. Negative feedback or low ratings can be a red flag. 10. Check for Licensing: Make sure that the lender has the appropriate license from the relevant financial regulatory authority to offer loans. 11. Report Suspicious Activities: If you suspect that a loan app or lender is targeting you with fraudulent practices, report it to your bank, local authorities, or financial regulators. By following these precautions, you can reduce the chances of falling victim to loan scams. Activity 4

Unit Entrepreneurship 3 Development Pic 3.1 Entrepreneurship is a deliberate, structured, and innovative process that involves initiating production, allocating resources, and identifying opportunities to yield profits and returns on investment while assuming the associated risks and uncertainties.

What is entrepreneurship? Entrepreneurship refers to the process of establishing and operating a new business venture, typically initiated by an individual. This individual is termed as an entrepreneur, and the organisation they establish is referred to as an enterprise. Individual Process Organisation Entrepreneur Entrepreneurship Enterprise

Traditionally, it was assumed that entrepreneurs were born with an innate ability to succeed in business. However, contemporary thinking suggests that entrepreneurship can be developed through a deliberate and systematic process. As a result, interested individuals can acquire the necessary skills and pursue entrepreneurship as a career path.Through training and education, students can be transformed into successful entrepreneurs. By recognizing entrepreneurship as a viable career path, individuals can make the transition from job seekers to job creators, thereby improving their 35 economic outlook and contributing to broader societal development..

Origin of the Word Entrepreneurship The term “entrepreneurship” originates from the French word “entreprendre,” which translates to “to undertake.” An entrepreneur is an individual who undertakes the production process by efficiently combining other factors of production, such as machinery, labour, and capital. Interestingly, the term “entrepreneur” was initially used in a military context to describe preparations for war. In the 18th century, French economist Richard Cantillon was the first to apply the term “entrepreneur” in an economic context, thereby introducing the concept of entrepreneurship to the field of economics. In the digital age, such scams are entering the scene in new ways! Here is where we need to realise the importance and scope of financial ethics. What is Financial Ethics? Financial ethics refers to the principles and values that should be followed in financial transactions. Financial ethics also emphasises considering the impact of financial decisions on others along with achieving financial aims . Financial ethics

promotes honesty, transparency, and responsible behavior in financial dealings. Financial ethics spans a variety of fields, including banking, investing, accounting, and personal finance. Key Ethical Principles in Finance In finance, ethics emphasise trust and transparency. These are critical for building strong relationships with stakeholders such as clients and investors. These principles include honesty, transparency, integrity, responsibility, confidentiality and trust. Honesty is a value to be followed in all financial transactions. Individuals or professionals should not misrepresent facts, make false promises or engage in fraudulent activities. Transparency means providing clear, accurate and easy information to clients. For example, transparent financial reporting helps investors make right decisions.

Responsibility is taking responsibility for one’s actions and their consequences. Finance professionals are responsible for ensuring accurate financial records and decisions that affect clients and investors. Financial professionals should emphasise to protect the interests of clients and the public by complying with the rules and regulations of financial activities. Confidentiality and trust must be maintained in the handling of financial information. Confidentiality refers to protecting sensitive financial information. Finance professionals often deal with clients’ personal and business details. This information must be kept secure and used only for authorised purposes. This is essential for long-term relationships with clients and investors. By upholding these principles, building trust among clients and the public, the financial sector needs to evolve towards a reliable, transparent and accountable financial system.

Ethics in Personal Finance Ethics in personal finance is just as important as professional financial ethics. Honesty and responsibility must be maintained in personal financial activities. These include being transparent about one’s financial situation, avoiding fraud

in financial transactions, and being honest about financial commitments. Ethical behavior in personal finance can build trust, prevent financial problems, and create a more sustainable and balanced approach to managing money. Let us discuss the important factors in this: 1. Responsible Financial Planning and Budgeting: This involves setting realistic goals. Make the right decisions. It all has to do with being careful about spending and saving. First of all, we need to prepare a financial budget that matches our short-term and long-term goals. Saving for future needs, avoiding unnecessary purchases and saving for emergencies are all virtues of planning. Responsible budgeting can improve financial stability, reduce debt and encourage disciplined spending.

2. Ethical Use of Debt and Loans: We should borrow only what we can practically repay and use loans only for productive purposes. Being careful with interest 48 rates, avoiding unnecessary debt and avoiding financial waste are all part of this. Ethical use of debt includes managing credit cards and other forms of debt responsibly. 3. Personal Responsibility in Managing Money: It is also important to take responsibility for good and bad financial decisions. This includes checking costs, admitting mistakes and making changes when necessary. Such responsibility builds financial discipline, promotes better decision-making, and fosters a sense of control over one’s financial dealings.

Financial Frauds and Irregularities Financial malpractices are intentional acts involving financial misappropriation and schemes aimed at deceiving others for financial gain. All these are considered as severe crimes in business and finance. Making personal gains and covering up poor performance are all financial irregularities. Such unethical trends can damage the trust, stability and reputation of financial systems and lead to serious legal and

financial consequences. Hope you have noticed various financial irregularities 1. Embezzlement: It involves the misappropriation of funds or assets entrusted to a person’s care. For example, an employee transfers company funds to personal accounts. 2. Insider Trading: It is the practice of illegal use of company’s confidential information by those within an organization (e.g. managers, employees) to conduct profitable transactions. It is making financial gains using strategic information. Which is not available to the outside world. 3. Ponzi Schemes: This is a type of investment fraudulence that pays dividends to previous investors by using the capital of new investors instead of making a profit. These schemes collapse when there will not be enough new investors. Eg: Money chains.

4. Accounting Fraud: There are those who manipulate financial records to 49 present a more favourable view of a company’s finances. Eg: Inflating profits or concealing liabilities to mislead investors. 5. Money Laundering: It is the process of disguising the source of ill-gotten gains through banking transactions or commercial transactions. It encourages tax evasion. . Avoid Scams and Deceptions in Digital Finance From phishing attacks to identity theft, opportunities for fraud and deceptions, abound in digital financial transactions. Users and organisations must be vigilant and educate themselves to identify fraudulent schemes, secure accounts, and implement legitimate practices. To monitor suspicious activity and provide clear reporting mechanisms, financial service providers need to take ethical steps such as educating users about potential risks. Digital Arrest Digital arrest is a specific type of cyber crime where scammers impersonate law enforcement officials and threaten victims with arrest if they don’t pay a fine or settle a fabricated debt. Scammers often create a sense of reality using fake arrest warrants and stolen phone numbers, sometimes utilising AI technology to simulate genuine circumstances, convincing victims they are under digital arrest.

Victims of digital arrest scams are threatened with exile, imprisonment, or severe consequences unless they transfer money into an account to settle the alleged charges. Such scams lead victims to lose money and personal information, while causing fear, anxiety, and significant financial loss. It’s important to remember that law

enforcement officials never ask for money over the phone or threaten arrest for non-payment. If you receive such a call, it is crucial to immediately notify the authorities. Phishing and Vishing Phishing and vishing are social media-based attacks used by cyber criminals to deceive individuals into sharing sensitive information. In phishing, fraudulent emails, messages, and specially designed websites are used for scams. Often, cybercriminals impersonate well-known companies or services. They trick victims into revealing crucial details such as login credentials and credit card numbers. For example, a victim receives an email that appears to be from their bank, asking them to confirm account details by clicking on a link. This 54 link redirects them to a fake page where the criminal steals their login information.

Vishing, or voice phishing, is a form of phishing that occurs over the phone. Scammers impersonate legitimate institutions such as banks or government agencies. They pressure victims into sharing personal or financial information. To make the call appear legitimate, they might use caller ID spoofing. For example, a person might receive a call claiming that suspicious activity has occurred in their bank account. The caller convinces the victim to provide their account number and PIN to “secure” the account. However, the true intention is to collect this information for fraudulent purposes.

Common Cybercrime Tactics 1. TRAI Phone Scam Some cyber criminals impersonate officials from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI), claiming that unlawful activities have been conducted or that KYC (Know Your Customer) norms have not been followed, threatening to temporarily suspend your mobile services. It’s important to note that only telecom companies have the authority to suspend services, not TRAI. 2. Parcel Held at Customs Some scammers make calls claiming that a parcel containing illegal items is stuck at customs. They then demand payment of a fine to release the parcel. Such calls should be reported to the authorities immediately. 3. Digital Arrest Scammers pose as police officers, threatening to question you over alleged criminal 55 activity. It’s important to remember that the police do not conduct digital arrests or online interrogations. 4.

Family Member Arrested Scammers claim that a family member or relative has been arrested and demand money for bail or legal proceedings. Before taking any action, you should contact your family member to verify the situation. 5. Get Rich Quick through Trading Some advertisements on social media promise high returns from certain stock investments. These are often scams with a high likelihood of fraud. Always be cautious when encountering such offers and conduct thorough research before investing. 6. Work-from-Home Scams Some scammers offer large payments for simple tasks, but they also ask for a security deposit. This is how they lure people into becoming victims of their fraud. Any scheme promising quick earnings is often a scam.

7. Lottery Scam If you receive a message or email claiming you’ve won a lottery and asking for your account details or a security deposit, it’s a scam. Never share your personal or financial details in such cases. 8. Incorrect Fund Transfer If you receive a call or message claiming that an incorrect amount has been credited to your account and asking for a refund, it could be a scam. Always verify such transactions with your bank. 9. KYC Expiry Scam Scammers impersonating bank representatives may call you or send links asking for KYC (Know Your Customer) updates. Banks usually do not contact you for KYC updates via calls or emails. Be cautious and recognize these as scams. 56 10. Tax Refund Scam Some scammers impersonate tax officials and ask for your bank details, claiming you’re entitled to a tax refund. Always ensure the authenticity of such claims before sharing any personal information. Activity 3

What is Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)? This is a concept whereby the business firms voluntarily integrate social and environmental services into their operations. Besides making profit, companies deal with the social and environmental challenges of the communities they operate in. CSR focuses on helping the communities where companies work. Its goal is to support sustainable development by ensuring that company’s operations are both profitable and beneficial to its shareholders. Importance of Corporate Social Responsibility in Business Activities towards social responsibility are essential in today’s business environment. What are the main reasons for that?

1. Brand Image and Reputation: Companies that are well-known through CSR activities increase customer loyalty and build good reputation. 2. Attract and retain talent: Employees are increasingly interested in working for socially responsible companies. 3. Investor attraction: Investors are more likely to support businesses that consider their social impact. 4. Compliance with laws: In many countries, rules require that companies engage in CSR activities. 5. Risk Management: CSR helps mitigate the risks associated with environmental issues, social concerns and government regulations. Overall, CSR helps create long-term value by aligning business practices with social good, ensuring a sustainable business model that benefits society. In short, these CSR projects demonstrate how companies can use their resources and influence to support social needs and environmental sustainability..

Legal Framework of CSR in India Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, companies are mandated to allocate at least 2% of their average net profit for the last three financial years towards CSR activities. In the previous financial year, this applies to companies with assets of Rs 500 crore or above / turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more / net profit of Rs 5 crore or more.
